ECE 6612

TLS identity and session keys

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how a certificate-authenticated TLS handshake connects an ephemeral shared secret to the intended server

Ephemeral Diffie–Hellman lets two peers compute a common secret from private contributions and public key shares. In finite-field notation, A = gᵃ mod p and B = gᵇ mod p give Bᵃ = Aᵇ = gᵃᵇ mod p. Modern TLS can instead use an elliptic-curve group.

An unauthenticated exchange can establish a secret with an impersonator. In the certificate-authenticated TLS 1.3 flow shown, the client validates the certificate for its intended server identity and verifies the server's CertificateVerify transcript signature. Certificate-path validation and application identity checking have complementary roles.

HKDF derives separate traffic keys using the shared secret and protocol context. Finished authenticates the handshake under a derived key, confirming the computed key material and transcript. Certificate authentication, ephemeral key agreement, and encrypted application records therefore remain separate steps.

Example

For an arithmetic-only illustration, p = 23 and g = 5 with private exponents 6 and 15 give public shares 8 and 19. Both compute the shared value 2. These tiny parameters illustrate the algebra and are unsuitable for real security.

Sources and scope
  • RFC 8446: TLS 1.3 key shares and authentication messages
  • RFC 5280: certification-path validation
  • RFC 5869: HKDF extract and expand

Practice

1. Why does proving that both ends computed a shared secret fail to establish the server's intended identity by itself?

An impersonator can participate in its own key exchange.

Key agreement alone identifies no trusted peer. Authentication must bind the transcript and key shares to the intended server, using the certificate/identity checks and proof of its private-key possession in this flow.

2. Why derive traffic keys instead of directly treating the raw Diffie–Hellman value as every encryption key?

Consider extraction, protocol context, and separate key uses.

A key-derivation schedule converts the shared material into appropriate keys and separates their purposes and directions. HKDF's context inputs bind the outputs to their intended protocol use.
